title: SQL Fundamentals
description: What SQL is, the little store database you'll use all course, and how to select, filter, sort, and clean up rows
prerequisites: None — this is the starting point

lessons.title: What is SQL & Relational Databases
lessons.description: Understand what SQL is for, how data is organized into tables, and the small store database you'll use all course

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a relational database is, why SQL exists, and read the sample schema you'll use throughout this course.

sections.title: 🗄️ What is a database, really?
sections.content:
A **database** is just an organized place to store data so it can be found again quickly and reliably. Instead of one giant spreadsheet, a **relational database** splits data into separate tables that relate to each other — one table for customers, one for orders, one for products, and so on.

**Why split it up?**
• Avoids repeating the same customer name on every single order
• Keeps each fact in exactly one place, so updates don't get out of sync
• Lets you combine tables however you need, on demand

**SQL** (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to a relational database: ask it questions, add data, change data, or remove data — all with plain, readable statements.

sections.title: 🏪 The little store you'll use all course
sections.content:
Every lesson in this course uses the same small, imaginary online store, so the examples build on each other instead of starting from scratch each time. Here's the whole schema — don't memorize it, just skim it once:

```sql
customers(customer_id, name, email, city, signup_date)
orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status)
order_items(order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
products(product_id, name, category, price, stock_qty)
employees(employee_id, name, department_id, salary, manager_id, hire_date)
departments(department_id, name)
```

**Reading a table definition:**
• The name outside the parentheses is the table (`customers`, `orders`, ...)
• The names inside are its columns
• `customer_id`, `order_id`, `product_id` are **keys** — unique IDs used to link tables together (you'll meet these properly in the joins module)

You'll see this exact schema referenced again and again, so it's worth a quick look now.

sections.title: 💡 SQL in one sentence
sections.content: Almost every SQL statement follows the same shape: **tell it what you want, and where to get it from.** The most common statement, `SELECT`, does exactly that — and it's what the next lesson is all about.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Thinking you need to memorize every table and column before starting — you don't, you'll pick them up lesson by lesson. Confusing a spreadsheet (one flat grid) with a relational database (many linked tables) — the whole point of splitting tables is to avoid repeating data.

questions.question: Why do relational databases split data into multiple tables instead of one big table?
options: To make queries harder to write
To avoid repeating the same data and keep each fact in one place
Because SQL cannot read large tables
It's only a historical convention with no real benefit
questions.explanation: Splitting data into related tables (customers, orders, products, ...) means each fact — like a customer's name — lives in exactly one place. That avoids duplication and keeps updates consistent.

questions.question: What does SQL stand for and what is it used for?
options: Structured Query Language — talking to a relational database
Simple Question Logic — writing conditional statements
System Quality Loop — testing software
Sequential Query List — ordering files
questions.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to ask questions of, and make changes to, a relational database.

questions.question: In the `orders` table, what is `customer_id` most likely used for?
options: It's just a random label with no purpose
It links each order back to the customer who placed it
It stores the customer's full name
It's the total price of the order
questions.explanation: customer_id is a key — an ID shared between the orders table and the customers table so you can connect an order back to the customer who placed it.

questions.question: What kind of database is SQL designed to work with?
options: A relational database, organized into tables with rows and columns
A single spreadsheet with no structure
A file system with folders only
An image storage system
questions.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is built specifically for relational databases, where data lives in related tables.

questions.question: What is a 'row' in a SQL table also called?
options: A record
A column
A schema
A join
questions.explanation: Each row in a table represents one record — one customer, one order, one product.

questions.question: What is a 'column' in a SQL table also called?
options: A field
A record
A row
A transaction
questions.explanation: Columns are the named fields that define what kind of data each row stores, like name or price.

questions.question: Why is splitting data into separate tables better than one giant table?
options: It avoids repeating the same customer info on every single order row
It makes queries impossible to write
It requires more storage with no benefit
It removes the need for any keys at all
questions.explanation: Separate tables mean each piece of information (like a customer's address) is stored once, not duplicated on every related row.

questions.question: Which of these is a relational database management system?
options: PostgreSQL
Microsoft Word
Photoshop
A text editor
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL is a widely used relational database system that runs SQL queries against structured tables.

lessons.title: Your First SELECT Query
lessons.description: Write your first SELECT statements to pull columns out of a table

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a SELECT statement that pulls specific columns — or all columns — out of a table.

sections.title: 🔍 SELECT ... FROM
sections.content:
Every basic query has two required parts: **what columns you want** (`SELECT`) and **which table to get them from** (`FROM`).

```sql
SELECT name, email
FROM customers;
```

This reads almost like English: "Select the name and email, from the customers table." The semicolon at the end just marks where the statement finishes.

sections.title: ⭐ Selecting everything
sections.content:
If you want every column, use `*` instead of listing them:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM products;
```

`*` is handy while you're exploring a table you don't know yet. Once you know what you actually need, listing specific columns is better — it's faster for the database, and clearer for anyone reading your query later.

sections.title: 🏷️ Renaming columns with AS
sections.content:
You can give a column a friendlier name in the results using `AS`:

```sql
SELECT name AS product_name, price AS unit_price
FROM products;
```

This doesn't change anything in the actual table — it only relabels the column in what you see back.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the FROM clause — SELECT always needs to know which table. Using SELECT * on huge tables in real applications, which pulls back far more data than needed and slows things down.

questions.question: Which query correctly selects the name and price columns from the products table?
options: GET name, price FROM products;
SELECT name, price FROM products;
SELECT products FROM name, price;
FROM products SELECT name, price;
questions.explanation: SELECT always lists the columns first, then FROM names the table: SELECT name, price FROM products;

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM customers; do?
options: Selects only the customer_id column
Deletes all rows from customers
Returns every column for every row in customers
Causes a syntax error
questions.explanation: The * wildcard means "all columns", so this returns every column for every row currently in the customers table.

questions.question: What does `SELECT name AS product_name FROM products;` do to the products table?
options: Permanently renames the name column to product_name
Nothing to the table — it only relabels the column in the query's results
Creates a new table called product_name
Deletes the name column
questions.explanation: AS only relabels a column in the output of that one query. The underlying table and its column names are unchanged.

questions.question: What does the `FROM` keyword specify in a SELECT query?
options: Which table to pull data from
Which columns to return
How to sort the results
How to filter the rows
questions.explanation: FROM tells the database which table the query is reading from.

questions.question: What does `SELECT *` mean?
options: Return every column in the table
Return zero columns
Return only the first row
Delete all rows
questions.explanation: The asterisk is a wildcard meaning 'all columns.'

questions.question: Is SQL case-sensitive for its keywords like SELECT and FROM?
options: No, but writing them in uppercase is a common convention for readability
Yes, keywords must always be lowercase
Yes, keywords must always be uppercase
SQL has no keywords at all
questions.explanation: SQL keywords are generally case-insensitive; uppercase is just a widely followed style convention.

questions.question: What ends a SQL statement in most database tools?
options: A semicolon (;)
A period (.)
A colon (:)
Nothing is needed
questions.explanation: The semicolon marks the end of a SQL statement, especially important when running multiple statements.

questions.question: What does `SELECT name FROM products;` return?
options: Just the name column for every row in the products table
Every column for every row
Just the first row's name
Nothing, since no WHERE clause is given
questions.explanation: Without a WHERE clause, every row is returned, but only the requested column (name) is shown.

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE
lessons.description: Narrow results down to only the rows you care about

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use WHERE with comparison operators, AND/OR, and IN to filter rows to exactly the ones you need.

sections.title: 🎯 Narrowing down rows with WHERE
sections.content:
`SELECT` picks columns; `WHERE` picks rows. It filters the table down to only the rows that match a condition:

```sql
SELECT name, city
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Chicago';
```

**Common comparison operators:**
• `=` equal to
• `!=` or `<>` not equal to
• `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` greater/less than
• `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` inside a range (inclusive)
• `LIKE '%pattern%'` matching text, where `%` means "anything"

sections.title: 🔗 Combining conditions with AND / OR
sections.content:
Chain multiple conditions together:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total_amount > 100;
```

`AND` means **both** conditions must be true; `OR` means **either** one is enough. Mixing them? Use parentheses to make the intent explicit:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND (total_amount > 100 OR customer_id = 42);
```

sections.title: 📋 Matching a list with IN
sections.content:
Checking a column against several values with a chain of ORs gets long fast. `IN` is the shortcut:

```sql
-- Instead of this:
WHERE city = 'Chicago' OR city = 'Austin' OR city = 'Denver'

-- Write this:
WHERE city IN ('Chicago', 'Austin', 'Denver')
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using = to compare against NULL (it never matches — you'll see the fix in the last lesson of this module). Forgetting quotes around text values ('Chicago', not Chicago). Writing AND when OR was actually meant, which silently returns zero rows.

questions.question: Which query returns orders with status 'shipped' AND a total over 50?
options: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped' OR total_amount > 50;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total_amount > 50;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status, total_amount > 50 = 'shipped';
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = shipped AND total_amount > 50;
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions to be true at once. Option D is also missing quotes around 'shipped', which would cause an error.

questions.question: What's the shortest way to write WHERE city = 'NYC' OR city = 'LA' OR city = 'SF'?
options: WHERE city BETWEEN 'NYC' AND 'SF'
WHERE city IN ('NYC', 'LA', 'SF')
WHERE city LIKE 'NYC, LA, SF'
WHERE city = 'NYC', 'LA', 'SF'
questions.explanation: IN checks a column against a list of values in one clean expression — equivalent to chaining the same comparison with OR, but far more readable.

questions.question: In WHERE status = 'shipped' AND (total_amount > 100 OR customer_id = 42), what does the parentheses do?
options: Nothing, they're purely decorative
Groups the OR condition so it's evaluated as one unit alongside the AND
Turns the query into a subquery
Causes a syntax error because AND and OR can't mix
questions.explanation: Parentheses group conditions, just like in math. Here they make sure "total_amount > 100 OR customer_id = 42" is evaluated together, and the result is combined with status = 'shipped' using AND.

questions.question: What does the WHERE clause do in a SELECT query?
options: Filters which rows are included in the result
Filters which columns are shown
Sorts the result set
Joins two tables together
questions.explanation: WHERE restricts the rows returned to only those matching the given condition.

questions.question: Which comparison operator checks for 'not equal to' in standard SQL?
questions.explanation: <> (and often != as well) is the standard SQL operator for inequality.

questions.question: What does `WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50` select?
options: Rows where price is between 10 and 50, inclusive
Rows where price is exactly 10 or exactly 50
Rows where price is less than 10
Rows where price is not 10 and not 50
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive of both boundary values.

questions.question: What does `WHERE name LIKE 'A%'` match?
options: Names starting with the letter A
Names ending with the letter A
Names containing the letter A anywhere
Names that are exactly 'A'
questions.explanation: The % wildcard in LIKE matches any sequence of characters, so 'A%' means 'starts with A.'

questions.question: What does the `NOT` keyword do in a WHERE clause?
options: Reverses the condition that follows it
Deletes rows matching the condition
Sorts the result in reverse order
Has no effect in SQL
questions.explanation: NOT negates the following condition, so WHERE NOT status = 'shipped' finds rows where status isn't 'shipped.'

lessons.title: Sorting, LIMIT, DISTINCT & NULLs
lessons.description: Order your results, cap how many rows come back, remove duplicates, and handle missing data

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use ORDER BY, LIMIT, DISTINCT, and IS NULL / IS NOT NULL together to shape a query's output.

sections.title: ↕️ Sorting with ORDER BY
sections.content:
By default, rows come back in no particular guaranteed order. `ORDER BY` sorts them:

```sql
SELECT name, total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
```

`ASC` (ascending, smallest first) is the default; `DESC` (descending, largest first) needs to be written explicitly. You can sort by more than one column — it sorts by the first, then breaks ties with the second, and so on.

sections.title: 🔢 Capping results with LIMIT
sections.content:
`LIMIT` caps how many rows come back — perfect for "top 5" style questions:

```sql
SELECT name, total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY total_amount DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

This pattern — ORDER BY then LIMIT — is one of the most common in real SQL: "give me the top N by some measure."

sections.title: 🧹 Removing duplicates with DISTINCT
sections.content:
`DISTINCT` collapses duplicate rows in the result down to one:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM customers;
```

Instead of one row per customer, this returns each city only once — handy for answering "which cities do we have customers in?"

sections.title: ❓ Handling missing data: NULL
sections.content:
`NULL` means **no value at all** — not zero, not an empty string, just unknown or missing. That's why `= NULL` never works; you can't check equality against "unknown". Use these instead:

```sql
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NULL;   -- finds employees with no manager

SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL;
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing WHERE manager_id = NULL — this silently returns nothing; use IS NULL. Assuming row order is guaranteed without an ORDER BY. Applying DISTINCT to the wrong column and being surprised the row count barely changed.

questions.question: Which query returns the 3 highest-value orders, largest first?
options: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount LIMIT 3;
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 3 ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
SELECT TOP 3 * FROM orders ORDER BY total_amount;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY total_amount DESC sorts largest first, and LIMIT 3 keeps only the first 3 rows of that sorted result.

questions.question: Why doesn't WHERE manager_id = NULL work as expected?
options: NULL must be written in lowercase as null
NULL means "unknown", and you can't test equality against unknown — IS NULL must be used instead
The manager_id column can never contain NULL
= NULL only works with text columns, not numbers
questions.explanation: NULL represents missing/unknown data, not a specific value, so equality comparisons against it don't behave the way you'd expect. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the correct way to test for it.

questions.question: What does SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers; return?
options: Every customer row, sorted by city
Only the first customer row
Each distinct city value once, with duplicates removed
The total count of customers per city
questions.explanation: DISTINCT collapses duplicate values in the result, so each unique city appears only once — it doesn't count or sort by itself.

questions.question: What does `ORDER BY price DESC` do?
options: Sorts rows by price from highest to lowest
Sorts rows by price from lowest to highest
Removes the price column
Filters out rows with no price
questions.explanation: DESC sorts in descending order; ASC (the default) sorts ascending.

questions.question: What does `LIMIT 5` do to a query's results?
options: Returns only the first 5 rows of the result
Returns rows where a column equals 5
Skips the first 5 rows
Limits the number of columns to 5
questions.explanation: LIMIT caps how many rows the query returns.

questions.question: Why does a NULL value need special handling in comparisons?
options: NULL represents 'unknown,' so ordinary equality checks like = NULL don't work as expected
NULL is just another way of writing zero
NULL cannot appear in a table at all
NULL always sorts before every other value automatically
questions.explanation: NULL means 'unknown' rather than a specific value, so you need IS NULL instead of = NULL.

questions.question: What is the correct way to check for NULL values in SQL?
options: IS NULL
= NULL
== NULL
NULL()
questions.explanation: SQL requires the special IS NULL syntax rather than an equality comparison.

questions.question: If two rows have the same price, what happens when you `ORDER BY price`?
options: Their relative order between each other is not guaranteed unless you add a tiebreaker column
The query fails with an error
One of the rows is automatically dropped
SQL always sorts ties alphabetically by name
questions.explanation: Without an additional ORDER BY column to break ties, rows with equal values can appear in any order.
